A goal about privacy. "In a child's hands", last sentence: "A child of 10 says what he or she wants to keep to himself or herself, and asks before sharing a photo of another person". The Dutch is "onderzoeken wat privacy is en hoe hiermee om te gaan in een veranderende samenleving": the verb is investigating, and the record's own Limits says the statement names "no technology, rule, law or situation and no way of dealing with privacy". "asks before sharing a photo of another person" is not investigating: it shows one way of dealing with privacy as what a child of 10 does, which reads as a rule of conduct the text does not give ("Common mistakes" then counts sharing photos of others without asking as the mistake). Show a child of 10 who investigates instead (for example one who finds out who can see a photo once it is shared), and give no rule. The rest of the illustration (listing what others can know, looking at the settings of an app or a form, asking an older person) is investigating, though it is set wholly in apps, accounts and chats, which the goal does not name. Wording and gloss are right. "In a child's hands" goes past what the statement names. The Dutch is "beseffen van het belang van (seksuele) integriteit": the verb is realising, an awareness goal, and the record's own Limits says it "names no parts of the body, situations or acts and sets no level of detail". The illustration then gives a script and rules of conduct as if they were the goal: "A child says which touch or closeness he or she wants and does not want, says "stop, I do not want that", and stops at once when another person says it. The child asks before touching someone, and accepts a "no" without asking for a reason", and for the child of 10 "that every person decides about his or her own body". That is a prescribed sentence, three rules and a scenario (touch) the text does not have, and it turns realising an importance into behaviour. It also settles what the gloss and Limits rightly leave open: *integriteit* is kept in Dutch with two readings (a person's inviolability, or acting uprightly; both are real, and "(seksuele)" stands in brackets), and the illustration shows only the first, in its bodily sense. Keep the illustration to a child who comes to see why integrity matters, with no sentence to say and no rule to follow. "Common mistakes" brings in a scenario of its own ("they must accept a touch from someone who is older or in charge"). The wording itself is right: the PDF prints the same sentence a second time, as the sixth dash of the fase 2 column of this cluster; the script's first place was that one, and the place given here is the printing in the fase 3 column. Limits, last sentence: "Price is not among the aspects it names." The Dutch is "aspecten als gezondheid, veiligheid en stevigheid (maar ook duurzaamheid) bij de keuze van een product": "aspecten als" opens a list of examples, as the same Limits says two sentences earlier ("given as examples of aspects"), so price falls inside the open list as much as any aspect that is not named; singled out, the sentence reads as a limit the wording does not set (the record's own "In a child's hands" has the child of 12 compare the aspects "with the price"). Say only that the list is open and names four aspects, or drop the sentence. The rest is right: wording equal on the page, and the gloss keeps *duurzaamheid* open (sustainability, or durability: both are real readings beside "stevigheid") and keeps "ervaren" as experiencing. Looked up on the page image of the content-line PDF (De samenleving, 04-2018, page 2): fase 3 column, cluster "Consument zijn", third dash; word for word equal to the record, nothing else in the dash.

Round 2 (ojw/ds/2/03/fase3). Round 1 (notes-contradict: "Price is not among the aspects it names", a limit the open list does not set) is resolved: Limits now ends "The list is open: the wording names these four aspects and does not give them as complete."
